mappings.note: How barter worked and what commodities it used. The goal covers the socio-economic role of institutions such as the market, which is where exchange without money belongs; no LO in this frame reaches money or barter.
The limitations of barter - double coincidence of wants, divisibility, durability. Economic reasoning under the goal.
The features of ancient Indian coins. Coins are historical evidence here, so the history goal rather than the economics one.
How the medium of exchange has changed over time, from commodities to digital money. The evolution of a market institution, so CG-SST4.
What made ancient Indian coins acceptable abroad - weight standards, metal purity, trade contact. A question about ancient coinage and commerce, so the history goal.
Reads the Arthashastra to work out the purchasing power of a pana and what a 100-pana fine implies about values. Inference from an ancient text, which is the history goal's sources clause.
A skit persuading people to accept cowrie shells as a medium of exchange - why a community agrees on money at all. Economic institution under the goal.
The RBI's sole right to print notes and the security features that protect them. The role of a government institution in the economy, which the goal names.

Interviewing family members and local shopkeepers about cash versus UPI is exactly the field-enquiry into how local shops work that LO-229 asks for. Not the bare goal, because the task is a field visit.
Defines barter as exchange of goods without money. Economic concept under the goal.
Sorts real barter commodities from one that was not used. Economic history of exchange under the goal.
The double coincidence of wants as barter's central difficulty. Economic reasoning under the goal.
Money's function as a medium of exchange. The core economic concept of the chapter.
The stone discs used as money on Yap. An example of what can serve as money, so the economics goal.
How money solves divisibility when an ox cannot be split. Economic reasoning under the goal.
The durability problem when perishables such as wheat are used for exchange. Economic reasoning under the goal.

Names barter as the system still practised at the Junbeel Mela. A recall about a surviving exchange practice, so the goal; the field-visit outcome is kept for items that ask learners to investigate a market themselves.
The feather material of the Solomon Islands tevau. Another example of commodity money under the goal.
A farmer with one ox and several needs, and how money resolves it. Economic reasoning under the goal.
Portability as a property required of money. Economic concept under the goal.

The Agni Puja that opens the Junbeel Mela. A detail of the barter fair the chapter uses as its living example, so the goal; no religion outcome applies because nothing about a religious movement is asked.
Defines a transaction. Economic vocabulary under the goal.
Identifies electronic bank-to-bank transfer among payment methods. Modern market institutions under the goal.
Commodity money having worth in itself against fiat money resting on trust and state backing. Economic reasoning under the goal.
Pricing a book illustrates money as a measure of value. A function of money under the goal.
What happens to a shell-money economy when the shells become scarce. Economic reasoning about the supply of money, so the goal.
Names minting as the making of coins. Economic vocabulary under the goal; the items about specific ancient coinages carry CG-SST2.
Defines an alloy as used in coinage. Technical vocabulary of money under the goal.
Karshapanas, also called punch-marked coins. Ancient Indian coinage, so the history goal.
The 'rupas' punched on ancient coins and the themes they carried. Reading ancient coins as evidence, so CG-SST2.
Defines the obverse of a coin. General numismatic vocabulary, so the economics goal rather than a point about a particular ancient coinage.
The Varaha and its reverse on Chalukya coins. A specific historical coinage, so CG-SST2.
Roman gold coins found in Pudukkottai read as evidence of long-distance trade. Archaeological inference, the history goal's clause.
Compares who minted coins in ancient times with the RBI's monopoly today. The modern half is the role of a government institution (CG-SST4), the ancient half is historical coinage (CG-SST2).
Matches an older currency unit to its value in rupees. The structure of a currency system, so the economics goal.
Why paper money replaced bulky coin. Economic reasoning about the form of money.
China as the first user of paper currency. Part of the evolution of money as an institution, so the goal.
Defines denominations. Economic vocabulary under the goal.
Digital money existing only as records against tangible coin and paper. Modern market institutions under the goal.
Expands 'QR code' in the context of digital payment. Modern payment practice under the goal.
